title: Origin of the alphabet
summary: Scholars trace most alphabets of the Near East and Europe, including Arabic and Latin, to the Proto-Sinaitic script, first found at Serabit el-Khadim in the Sinai in 1905 and 1906. Inscriptions near ancient Thebes, announced in 1999, suggest that traders or mercenaries were writing in simplified Egyptian hieroglyphs around 1900 to 1800 BCE. Few early texts can be read, and their nature remains open to interpretation.

uncertainty.note: Encyclopedia.com notes Semitic traders or mercenaries began writing in simplified hieroglyphs around 1900 to 1800 BCE as discovered at Wadi el-Hol; World History Encyclopedia dates the Proto-Sinaitic script at Serabit el-Khadim to around 1700 BCE.

as_recorded.value: some time around 1900 to 1800 b.c.e., began to write their own language in a system of simplified Egyptian hieroglyphs
Proto-Sinaitic script is thought by some to have been developed in central Egypt around 1700 BCE

when.display: c. 1900–1700 BCE (Middle Bronze Age / Egyptian Middle Kingdom)

where.modern_name: Serabit el-Khadim, South Sinai, Egypt (early inscriptions; origin debated)
where.historical_name: Serabit el-Khadim turquoise mining zone and Hathor temple precinct, southwestern Sinai (Egyptian Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty)

importance.justification: The invention of the consonantal alphabet replaced elite scribal logographies with an easily learned phonetic system that became the direct ancestor of nearly all modern alphabets worldwide.

related.because: The alphabetic principle originated as an inventive simplification of Egyptian hieroglyphic and hieratic writing systems by Semitic speakers in contact with Egyptian scribes.
